postponable.BET-15: Rejected as framed; replaced by BET-18.

reviews.rationale: No independent outcome exists for any data layer: ARCH's outcome evidence is a preprint that A6 did not open, and the one Takeda outcome claim (about 30% shorter narcolepsy trial development, from the then-CEO's January 2026 interview) has no baseline or method. That Takeda's estate is fragmented is itself an unverified hypothesis. Backs the bet only because the decision log makes the claim testable.
reviews.unresolved: Whether any named decision can be baselined by end-2027 (the bet's own stop test); IVB-001.

reviews.rationale: Lowest engineering risk of the AI-related bets. A Databricks-hosted agent platform for 10,000+ employees already exists and ARCH was built by fewer than ten full-time staff plus contractors. Catalogue, metadata standard and decision log are commodity components, so the risk is adoption, not engineering. Caveat: platform maturity is vendor self-report ('capacity of the audience, not agents in production').
reviews.unresolved: Count of data and AI products in production versus pilot (IVB-001).

reviews.rationale: No revenue or cost line is tied to the layer and the capital file says rNPV is not meaningful. Lilly's equivalent asset is experimental data company-estimated at over USD 1bn, which a governance layer over existing trial data does not replicate. Commercial value is cheaper or faster decisions, which has to be shown at gate 3 (RM-015, 2027 H2).
reviews.unresolved: Which franchise decision is the first baselined use; whether Takeda trial data are reusable under existing consents.

reviews.rationale: USD 200m over 14 years is about 4% of the balanced envelope and a small fraction of base R&D (JPY 675.9bn in FY2025). Stage-gated with a 2027 stop test. Main risk is sunk-cost persistence ('platform spend hard to stop'), so the stop criterion must bind.
reviews.unresolved: Run cost after scale (ASM-101 is a sizing assumption anchored on one competitor's headcount).

reviews.rationale: FDA's January 2025 draft credibility framework applies where models inform regulatory decisions. Reuse of de-identified trial data across franchises needs a consent review (ARCH excluded prison and paediatric populations) and cross-border transfer rules for Japan, EU and US data; the bet analyses neither. Takeda's own 20-F warns models may be flawed or trained on inadequate data.
reviews.unresolved: Consent scope of legacy Takeda trials for secondary use.

reviews.rationale: Competitors cannot take this away because it is internal, but it also creates no advantage they cannot copy: ARCH took under ten staff. It is hygiene that makes other bets testable, not a moat. Conditional on being presented as enabling infrastructure and not as differentiation.
reviews.unresolved: Whether Takeda's data are more decision-relevant than rivals' (no public evidence).

reviews.rationale: Class 9 is EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED with a named CDTO and an insourced digital workforce, so extension is feasible. The same CDTO also owns BET-08 and supplies the platform BET-17 measures, during a CEO transition (24 June 2026) and a cost programme with about 4,500 role reductions per trade press. Conditional on IVB-001 showing the platform is not already doing this work.
reviews.unresolved: Whether a second function adopts the standard within 12 months (stage-gate stop test).

reviews.rationale: The science is process science: whether adaptive nomograms and AI process models raise yield per litre. Takeda gives no yield, productivity or cost figures. The sharpest objection is in the bet's own data: H1 FY2026 plasma revenue was -1.5% at constant rates (+8.5% at actual rates), which does not look capacity-bound; if demand rather than capacity limits sales, yield gains deliver cost savings only.
reviews.unresolved: Yield per litre and cost per litre by centre (IVB-006); whether plasma is demand- or capacity-bound.

reviews.rationale: No public evidence of Takeda lab, continuous-manufacturing or manufacturing robotics. Automating GMP fractionation needs validated change control and Takeda has a documented warning letter and supply shortage. 170+ predictive-maintenance agents at Lessines are a positive sign but carry no outcome. Fixed-price, outcome-linked vendor terms are a NEEDS_MORE_RESEARCH hypothesis and the SpaceX cost-gap analogue is not causally isolated by its own source.
reviews.unresolved: Whether any vendor accepts outcome-linked terms at plasma plant complexity (stage-gate stop test).

reviews.rationale: Immunoglobulins are JPY 790.6bn (18% of revenue) and sit outside the biosimilar mechanism, the strongest part of the thesis. The revenue test is missing: PDT revenue +8.5% AER but -1.5% CER in H1 FY2026. 'No competitor holds this data' is true only because the comparison set (Lilly, J&J, AbbVie) has no plasma business; dedicated plasma companies are not in the registry. Value is cost per litre, which is unknown.
reviews.unresolved: Cost per litre versus plasma peers (not public).

reviews.rationale: USD 430m is the third-largest funded line and sits on top of a USD 230m Los Angeles expansion that has no commissioning data. Back the USD 50-65m baseline-and-shadow-mode tranche. Do not pre-commit the USD 200m H2 and USD 150m H3 tranches until measured headroom clears ASM-031, which is an illustrative 2% with no economic anchor.
reviews.unresolved: Value of a 2% yield or cost gain (needs IVB-006 data).

reviews.rationale: GMP validation of automated steps; prior warning letter, shortage and a USD 505m damages award; current inspection status unknown. Ethics gap: personalised nomograms change donation volume and frequency, and the registry holds no donor-welfare analysis. The neutral-capacity extension raises unresearched competition-law and liability questions.

Opposes the 'unique data' premise: the registry cannot say what plasma peers do with process data, and neither does the bet. Competitors in the registry are irrelevant here and the competitors that matter are unresearched. A cost-per-litre case may still stand, but the data-moat framing is unsupported.
reviews.unresolved: Peer benchmark of plasma yield and automation (public-knowledge gap).

reviews.rationale: Best fit to a public Takeda strength: 270+ centres, a USD 230m expansion, 99.6% on-time in-full, and a CEO who previously led the Plasma-Derived Therapies unit. Execution risk is quality, not sponsorship (Hikari history).

Orzeyful (oveporexton), approved 2026-08-05, is a credible in-house result, but the same franchise produced TAK-994, stopped for a liver-related signal. Second-asset approval is ASM-021 at 15% (range 5-30%). The bet's own competition line says other orexin programmes were 'not researched'. The platform claim needs two approvals, and the stage gate withdraws it if only one exists after 2040.
reviews.unresolved: Competitor orexin pipeline (not in registry); IVB-008 early-pipeline depth.

reviews.rationale: Capability is demonstrated in-house: oveporexton was discovered in Shonan and has Phase 2 and Phase 3 publications. The bet needs candidate chemistry and safety screening, not new technology. AI design (BET-07) is an optional accelerator, not a dependency.

Narcolepsy type 1 is a rare indication and platform value needs further indications; the indication map is RM-008 (2027 H1) and does not yet exist. Launch is gated by a DEA scheduling decision. Regeneron's EYLEA -42% shows a platform does not protect a product, only repeated assets do.
reviews.unresolved: Indication map beyond NT1; payer terms for NT1.

reviews.rationale: Opposes USD 500m: 17% of the balanced envelope for PTS 0.1-0.3 and 8-12 years to payoff; RM-048 puts platform proof at 2038, after the Entyvio erosion window (ASM-025 2031 plus three years). The spend is called incremental to base R&D (ASM-035), but an orexin discovery team in Shonan is already in base R&D (JPY 675.9bn), so additionality cannot be tested. Would back the USD 300m constrained size with a Phase 1 gate before releasing H2.
reviews.unresolved: What share of the USD 500m is already inside base R&D (IVB-014).

reviews.rationale: Liver-safety history raises the safety bar for any follow-on orexin agonist. Orzeyful is lawful to market only after a DEA scheduling decision, so abuse liability and scheduling are open for the class. No registry evidence on label restrictions or risk-management requirements.
reviews.unresolved: DEA scheduling outcome and its effect on launch.

reviews.rationale: A competitor orexin scan is missing from the bet and from the registry, so the red team cannot rate Takeda's head start. First-approval advantage is real but lasts only until a cleaner follower reaches the same indications. Conditional on that scan before the H2 tranche.
reviews.unresolved: Competitor orexin programmes and their phase.

reviews.rationale: Supported by public capability: Shonan discovery, in-house origin and late-stage delivery against the 2024 R&D Day plan. Takeda has stopped programmes decisively (TAK-994, soticlestat, cell therapy). Risk: the JPY 200bn programme competes for R&D headcount and early-pipeline depth beyond six late-stage assets is unknown.

The scientific content is real-world persistence and comparative evidence. No company publishes adherence or persistence outcomes, so the evidence plan has no benchmark. The pediatric sBLA (PDUFA Q1 2027) and the SC pen are real lifecycle assets, and Entyvio grew 2.7% at constant rates in H1 FY2026, so the franchise is not yet eroding.
No technology risk: payer analytics and contracting capability, not new infrastructure.

Largest dated exposure: Entyvio JPY 958.0bn (21% of revenue), Medicare negotiation effective January 2028, two biosimilar BLAs under FDA review and a PBM template precedent from Stelara. Supports spending ahead of dated events. Notes that cost is tiny against exposure, so the open question is whether contracting changes net outcome at all.
reviews.unresolved: Size of the contractable (pharmacy-benefit) share of Entyvio.

reviews.rationale: USD 140m against JPY 383-766bn of annual revenue at risk (ASM-024 on the global base) is the cheapest line relative to exposure in the portfolio. Money is not the binding constraint, so the council would raise funding if a specific lever with measurable effect is named.

The Medicare negotiated price is statutory, so contracting cannot offset it. Rebate-for-access, co-brand and patient-programme designs sit under anti-kickback and copay-accumulator rules. Co-brand private-label arrangements draw scrutiny that the bet has not researched.
reviews.unresolved: Compliance review of any co-brand or rebate design.

reviews.rationale: Backs the spend but not the premise that contracting retains revenue. AbbVie kept at least 97% of Humira volume to March 2024 through rebate-for-access, yet global Humira fell 78.6% in three years. AbbVie and J&J already sell competing IBD products (Skyrizi and Rinvoq in UC and Crohn's, Tremfya in Crohn's). PBM private-label biosimilars route around contracts. The analogues are pharmacy-benefit drugs; whether Entyvio IV is mainly medical benefit is not in the registry.
reviews.unresolved: Medical versus pharmacy benefit split of Entyvio (IVB-004).

reviews.rationale: Capability gap is documented: patient services and market access is an EVIDENCE_GAP, US revenue fell 9.0% at actual rates in FY2025, and the owning US unit is also preparing three launches. The new CEO is a former US unit head, which helps sponsorship. Conditional on named contracting leadership before RM-003 (2027 H1).
reviews.unresolved: Named owner and contracting team size.

reviews.rationale: Strongest clinical evidence among the funded bets: two positive Phase 3 psoriasis studies (about 70% sPGA 0/1 at week 16) and head-to-head superiority over deucravacitinib on PASI 100. PsA Phase 3 completes May 2027. Efficacy statements are company-reported.
No technology risk. Takeda met the December 2024 R&D Day plan for the first three assets on time.

Psoriasis is crowded: J&J's oral IL-23 peptide Icotyde was approved 2026-03-17 with head-to-head superiority claims, and Skyrizi and Tremfya are entrenched. Zasocitinib replaces revenue; it does not succeed Entyvio in GI. The USD 10-20bn peak estimate is not probability-adjusted. Two USD 1.0bn milestones are payable at USD 4bn and USD 5bn annual net sales.

USD 180m incremental on a USD 4.0bn sunk asset has the highest marginal return in the portfolio because the base asset exists. The council asks whether it is under-funded relative to BET-03 and BET-06.
reviews.unresolved: Incremental indications that clear a Phase 2 bar.

reviews.rationale: The FDA action date was not captured. Inspection findings, not clinical data, caused CRLs at Lilly and AbbVie, and Takeda's quality record includes Hikari. Third-party sites sit in the supply chain.
reviews.unresolved: Inspection status of sites supporting the NDA (IVB-011).

reviews.rationale: Competitor response is the central risk: oral and injectable IL-23 products with head-to-head data are marketed in psoriasis already and zasocitinib's head start is only against deucravacitinib. Conditional on payer coverage at 6 and 12 months (stage gate) and on tracking, not forecasting, replacement of Entyvio exposure.

Delivery to date is strong, but class 8 launch execution is POTENTIAL_NEW_CAPABILITY and three launches fall within 12 months of June 2026 while restructuring expense runs at JPY 128.1bn (FY2024), JPY 70.8bn (FY2025) and about JPY 160bn (FY2026 revised).

No option from the window has produced an approved product. Neuroscience, gene and cell therapy concentrate write-downs (emraclidine USD 4.5bn, Takeda cell therapy JPY 58.2bn), and Denali and Neurocrine collaborations ended. The RNAi-next-to-fazirsiran idea is plausible but the bet names no target.
reviews.unresolved: Target modality and disease-depth map (stage-gate discovery).

reviews.rationale: Needs modality-specific diligence that is not evidenced: Takeda Ventures and Center for External Innovation scope is an EVIDENCE_GAP. The deal-outcome scorecard that would discipline the engine does not exist yet (RM-007, 2027 H1).

Differentiation is 'low to moderate' in the capital file: others license similar assets and AbbVie spends USD 0.6-1.0bn a year on early upfronts and options. Takeda would bid with a USD 700m 14-year envelope against deeper pockets. PTS 0.05-0.15 and commercial probability 0.4-0.6 make expected value low and unquantified.
reviews.unresolved: Win rate against competing bidders for the same assets.

reviews.rationale: Opposes USD 700m: second-largest line (24% of balanced) with 7-12 years to payoff (RM-043: first option-sourced approval 2035), so it does not bridge the 2031-34 Entyvio window. It is also smaller than one Innovent-type licence (USD 1.2bn upfront), so it neither replaces nor funds the licence path Takeda actually uses. Would back a USD 150-300m scorecard-first tranche.
reviews.unresolved: Where Phase 2/3 licences of USD 0.5-2bn are funded (no bet covers them).

reviews.rationale: Antitrust and cross-border review is not researched, including China-sourced licences of the Innovent type. Contingent value rights and milestone structures need accounting and disclosure care.
reviews.unresolved: Cross-border review for China-sourced assets (not in registry).

reviews.rationale: Rivals already hold new-modality positions and bid for the same assets (AbbVie ADARx USD 335m upfront with up to USD 7.5bn milestones; Lilly Verve). Takeda's edge must be selection and late-stage execution, which is evidenced for Nimbus and Protagonist but not for early options.
reviews.unresolved: Takeda hit rate on early assets.

reviews.rationale: Deal flow is a public strength (four of six late-stage programmes externally sourced) and Takeda has terminated programmes decisively. The organisation behind early options is undocumented, and a CEO transition plus role cuts fall first on corporate functions.
reviews.unresolved: Corporate development capacity and CVR/option experience (IVB-007).

reviews.rationale: Outcome evidence is mixed at best: Recursion ended four of 11 programmes, rentosertib's Phase IIa showed an FVC signal with seven liver-related discontinuations, and AI-origin Phase 2 success is cited as about conventional (secondary citation). Nabla's three-to-four-week loop is a CEO statement to Reuters. No Takeda outcome is disclosed. The first-in-human gate is the right test.
reviews.unresolved: Nabla first-in-human data (company expectation: one to two years from October 2025).

reviews.rationale: Models converge on shared open models, weakening any model-level edge. Dependency wiring is inconsistent: the bets file lists BET-01 and BET-09 as hard prerequisites, but roadmap gate RM-011 (Nabla first-in-human window, 2027 H2) depends only on RM-007, while the BET-01 decision-log gate (RM-015, 2027 H2) and the BET-09 cost benchmark (RM-018, 2028 H1) are not upstream of it. Data could arrive before a comparator exists.
reviews.unresolved: Whether a conventional-candidate comparator exists when Nabla data arrive.

reviews.rationale: Opposes the moat claim: partners compound unless Takeda keeps data ownership, success-based payments above USD 1bn per deal are contingent liabilities, and commercial probability is 0.3-0.5. Tech-native partners serve Takeda's rivals in parallel (Isomorphic reportedly raised USD 600m; Lilly has Isomorphic, Chai and OpenAI).
reviews.unresolved: Contract terms on data ownership and feedback into partner models.

reviews.rationale: USD 180m with a first-in-human gate is a fair option price against reference deals (Isomorphic USD 45m upfront, BigHat USD 30m). Back the USD 40m H1 tranche. Release USD 80m H2 and USD 60m H3 only on RM-020 (2028 H2) evidence.
reviews.unresolved: Committed versus contingent payments in the Nabla and Iambic contracts (undisclosed).

reviews.rationale: FDA's credibility framework is draft. AI-designed molecules still face the standard safety package, and rentosertib shows liver signals can appear. Data leakage and IP ownership terms in partner contracts are stated as a risk but cannot be reviewed.

Opposes as a differentiator: Lilly has Isomorphic, Chai, OpenAI and NVIDIA compute; AbbVie has BigHat and Valkai; the AISB consortium gives five pharmas the same fine-tuned model. A Takeda alliance with Nabla or Iambic is access to a model that rivals can also buy. Value exists only if Takeda's proprietary assay data are the differentiator, which makes this a feature of BET-01 and BET-09, not a separate bet.

Alliances exist (Nabla 2022 and 2025, Iambic 2026) with no outcome disclosed. Takeda's stop discipline is evidenced in portfolio decisions (TAK-994, soticlestat, cell therapy), which supports feasibility. Conditional on stop rules being written into contracts before the next payment.

The only measured result is vendor-organised: about 10 points better pose accuracy on 1,056 private held-out structures, not peer reviewed. Whether it helps Takeda targets is untested; that is the bet's own gate.
reviews.unresolved: Held-out gain on Takeda targets (RM-006, 2027 H1).

reviews.rationale: Takeda has been a member since 2025-10-01, the infrastructure (Apheris) exists and held-out evaluation on Takeda data is straightforward.
Access is pooled and non-exclusive, so it buys parity, not advantage; the bet itself says the moat is the internal decision layer. Takeda is not on the AISB Bind founding list.
reviews.unresolved: Which tasks Takeda would federate beyond structure prediction.

reviews.rationale: USD 35m, reversible and measurable in 2027 H1. Best capital efficiency in the AI set.
Federated learning between competitors needs a competition-law review of information flows and clean IP terms. Privacy and consent limit pooling. Neither is analysed.
reviews.unresolved: Competition-law opinion on consortium data flows.

reviews.rationale: Takeda is a follower in every consortium: AbbVie and J&J are founding partners of AISB Bind and Takeda is not, and Lilly's TuneLab reaches 1,300+ biotechs through Benchling. Acceptable at this price; unacceptable as a strategy.
Already a member, owned by the CDTO, low organisational load.

Stage 1-2 automation is commodity. The scientific question is whether AI-planned experiments beat human-planned ones prospectively, which no source shows. The 'rent, do not own' evidence partly rests on Lilly's sale of its Studio, whose reason is undisclosed and whose start date (2017 or about 2020) and Strateos link are disputed.
reviews.unresolved: Prospective AI-planned versus human-planned comparison on the same target.

reviews.rationale: Technically mature: Arctoris runs the former Lilly platform as a CRO and expanded biophysics capacity ten-fold. Risks are interfaces, data schema and quality, manageable through acceptance criteria.

Anyone can rent the same capacity, including AI-biotech rivals (Arctoris sells data generation to AI customers). The only asset Takeda owns is its schema and assay choice. Commercial probability 0.5-0.8 is cost avoidance against an unknown internal baseline (IVB-002).
USD 95m, service model, no fixed capital, with a cost-against-internal-baseline gate at RM-018 (2028 H1). The right instrument for an option on stage 3.

Data-integrity standards (GLP or GxP), audit rights and IP and data-ownership terms with a CRO are unstated. Vendor concentration risk if one provider dominates; the sector's rented-lab model is described as commercially fragile.

Accepts rent over own but contests the premise. Lilly sold the Studio in 2024 and in 2026 announced a joint lab of up to USD 1bn with NVIDIA, which reads as re-platforming at larger scale, not retreat. Zymergen, an industrial-biotech company, is a weak analogue for drug-discovery automation. If Lilly's new lab works, renting leaves Takeda a follower; the ladder triggers are the hedge.
reviews.unresolved: Whether the Lilly-NVIDIA lab is operating (CLM-006007 says no outcome reported).

reviews.rationale: Low organisational load, no capability to build, owned by the Head of R&D. One inconsistency: the bets file lists no prerequisite, but roadmap RM-005 (CRO contract) depends on RM-002 (data standard), which depends on RM-001 (BET-17 inventory).
reviews.unresolved: Whether RM-005 can start before RM-001.

reviews.rationale: Endorses REJECT. No independent demonstration of closed-loop autonomous discovery with a clinical outcome exists in any source opened; failure modes and reproducibility are unstudied.
Endorses REJECT. Stage 4-5 is not demonstrated. The Lilly-NVIDIA lab is at concept and the Medicine Foundry is under construction.
Endorses REJECT. No revenue case; commercial probability 0.1-0.3.
Endorses REJECT. Zero allocation, and watching the triggers is free.
Endorses REJECT. Acceptability of autonomously generated data for submissions is unsettled under the draft FDA credibility framework.

Accepts zero spend but disputes the stated evidence: 'two owned-model failures' is one divestiture of undisclosed cause plus one company from another sector. Lilly is spending more on owned wet labs, not less. The trigger set (independent Lilly result, Nabla first-in-human, CRO cost) is a NEEDS_MORE_RESEARCH hypothesis and must be written so a Lilly success actually moves Takeda.
reviews.unresolved: Operationalised triggers with dates and owners.

reviews.rationale: Endorses REJECT. No lab-automation evidence at Takeda and no capacity to absorb a new capability during restructuring.

Convenience formats raise access, but no persistence or outcome data exist for Takeda or competitors. Whether SC users persist longer or hold share after biosimilar entry is untested; the capital file says the effect after entry is not established.
Capability exists: SC pen approvals and the HYHUB 510(k) clearance. J&J's OTTAVA impairment is a robotics counter-example, not a drug-device one.

Conflicts with BET-04: SC pens move patients into the pharmacy benefit, which is where PBM private-label biosimilar templates operate. Whether the pen protects net price is open, and IV-to-SC cannibalisation before exclusivity loss is a stated risk. The bet is labelled evidence_backed although its supporting interpretation is PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED.
reviews.unresolved: Net price per SC versus IV patient.

reviews.rationale: USD 190m at high capital efficiency, subject to the 2027 H2 baseline (RM-013). Device capex competes with core spending.
reviews.unresolved: Device capex share of the USD 190m.

reviews.rationale: Combination-product and 510(k) pathways are familiar to Takeda. Human-factors and recall risk are sector-wide.

SC is table stakes: Tremfya, Skyrizi and Rinvoq are convenient and sit in the same prescriber base. Biosimilars in review are IV, so SC protection rests on patents and device IP, which do not outlast the drug's exclusivity.
Existing strength: pen and HYHUB are approved and Takeda says SC drives uptake. Moderate load on the US unit.

No company publishes adherence, persistence or time-to-therapy outcomes, so there is no benchmark. Help at Hand's 100,000 patients is an enrolment count. That pathways limit oveporexton uptake is a NEEDS_MORE_RESEARCH hypothesis.
reviews.unresolved: Time from prescription to first dose (baseline).

reviews.rationale: Measurement and partnership work, not technology.

Pear Therapeutics shows reimbursement, not evidence, decides standalone digital support, so support attached to the drug is the right structure. AbbVie's revised Allē programme was reversed within months. Value is learning for the 2027-28 launches and is not quantifiable.
reviews.unresolved: Payer willingness to reimburse pathway services.

reviews.rationale: USD 100m is large for an experiment in measurement. The USD 30m H1 tranche is reasonable; the USD 70m H2 and H3 balance should be contingent on RM-021 (2028 H2). Would cap at USD 50m until a pathway bottleneck is shown.
The most compliance-exposed EXPERIMENT: anti-kickback and copay-accumulator rules constrain hub design, hub data ownership is unknown and patient data need consent.

Competitor launches were governed by certification and capacity: Spravato (site-limited) and Carvykti (capacity-bound), not by hubs. Timing: oveporexton was approved 2026-08-05 while the pathway pilot is dated 2027 H2 (RM-012) and reports in 2028 H2 (RM-021), so the first-year launch curve forms before the pilot reports.
reviews.unresolved: Date of oveporexton commercial availability (DEA scheduling).

reviews.rationale: Class 8 launch execution is POTENTIAL_NEW_CAPABILITY and class 14 patient services is an EVIDENCE_GAP. Owner is the US Patient Services head inside the same US organisation that carries three launches and the January 2028 Entyvio price. Conditional on one named launch and one named leader.
Registry data can support evidence generation, but the cited regulatory-use example is a vendor snippet and Flatiron's value rests on oncology EHR scale that Takeda's areas lack.
Needs consent, interoperability and governance that BET-01 will not deliver before about 2029. No Takeda data network is public.

Disputes carrying USD 80m: Flatiron's value is neutrality (Roche kept it a separate entity), and a single-pharma sponsor undermines it. Commercial probability is 0.2-0.4 with no demand evidence. Should be zero-funded until a neutral sponsor exists.

Disputes inconsistent treatment: BET-13 is DEFER yet carries USD 80m in the balanced and USD 160m in the ambitious envelope, while the other DEFER bet (BET-15) is excluded. Would remove the line and fund a USD 25m options paper (RM-028, 2029 H2) from BET-12.
reviews.unresolved: Whether the USD 80m is counted in the USD 2,950m total (it is).

reviews.rationale: Consent, neutrality and cross-border privacy for rare-disease patients are unresearched.
Endorses DEFER: competitors will contribute only to a neutral registry and none exists; nothing is lost by waiting until 2029.
Disputes: Takeda has no data-network capability and the class is POTENTIAL_NEW_CAPABILITY. Bandwidth is consumed by the cost programme and three launches.
Endorses REJECT. No measured internal advantage to productise.
Endorses REJECT. Federated participation (BET-08) gives the only technology exposure that is warranted.
Endorses REJECT. Customers are rivals, TuneLab has disclosed no uptake, and NVIDIA's own filing warns customers with in-house capability replace platform layers.
Endorses REJECT. Lilly's data cost is over USD 1bn; Takeda cannot show comparable data volume.
Endorses REJECT. Sharing models or data with competing biotechs raises unresearched competition-law, privacy and IP exposure.
Endorses REJECT. Lilly is two years ahead with Benchling distribution to 1,300+ customers.
Endorses REJECT. Class 9 is EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED with no outcome evidence.
Agrees on requiring Phase 2+ data, but AbbVie's Cerevel purchase (a 54% write-down, emraclidine USD 4.5bn) shows Phase 2 CNS data do not de-risk.
Endorses DEFER. Nothing technical depends on it.
The replacement gap is unmeasured without launch curves, and the USD 10-20bn peak is not probability-adjusted, so whether a bridge is needed cannot be shown from public data.

Agrees nothing is funded, but the trigger arithmetic is already unmet. A USD 5bn purchase is JPY 750bn at ASM-001. Adjusted net debt JPY 3,817.6bn over EBITDA JPY 1,457.2bn is 2.6x; adding JPY 750bn gives about 3.13x before the Amitiza provision and about 3.41x if the JPY 403.5bn provision is also debt-funded, against the 3.0x ceiling (council arithmetic, ignores free cash flow and acquired earnings). DEFER hides that the purchase is infeasible without deleveraging.
reviews.unresolved: Free cash flow after dividends (IVB-012, IVB-014).

reviews.rationale: Antitrust review of a USD 5bn deal is not researched.

Disputes DEFER: AbbVie (ImmunoGen plus Cerevel, USD 17.5bn net) and J&J (USD 17.5bn in FY2025) bought bridges. Entyvio exposure of JPY 383-766bn a year exceeds what USD 180m of BET-05 breadth can offset. If assets are bid away while Takeda waits for 2031 triggers, the bridge is gone. Asks for a funded USD 0.5-2bn Phase 2/3 licence channel instead of a binary USD 5bn trigger.

Takeda stated no significant acquisitions in the three years to March 2026 and its one large purchase (Nimbus) has delivered. Capacity is limited by leverage, Amitiza and a progressive dividend policy. Conditional on the CFO and new CEO setting leverage policy first.
Endorses REJECT. No clinical rationale.
Endorses REJECT. Would require a direct channel Takeda does not run.
Endorses REJECT. Takeda's products are infused, specialty or plasma-derived. Lilly gives no revenue share for LillyDirect.
Endorses REJECT. Zero allocation.
Endorses REJECT. Copay-accumulator and anti-kickback rules limit combining discounts with insurance. Whether Takeda holds a government pricing agreement is not in the registry.
Endorses REJECT. A cash-pay channel in a category with an uninsured gap is Lilly's advantage, not available to Takeda's specialty products.
Endorses REJECT. Class 14 is an EVIDENCE_GAP and the US organisation is already loaded.

J&J's 10-15% of use cases driving about 80% of value is one CIO interview, and the 2.6x enrolment gain has no baseline. Takeda's 63.4% workforce AI use and 30.9% course take-up are adoption metrics. The only Takeda outcome claim is single-source.
Measurement and advisory-only decision support; low technical risk.

No revenue line; value is pruned spend. Attribution is the issue: the JPY 200bn gross savings target mixes technology with about 4,500 role reductions. IVB-003 is meant to separate them, but the stage-gate owner is the CFO, who is also accountable for the savings.
reviews.unresolved: Share of savings attributable to technology.

reviews.rationale: USD 120m is 4% of the envelope for a measurement office, decision support and reskilling, while ARCH shows platform-class work done by under ten staff. Back USD 40m in H1; make H2 contingent on measured use cases (RM-023, 2029 H1).
reviews.unresolved: Split of USD 120m between measurement, tools and reskilling.

reviews.rationale: Reskilling and role reductions interact with works councils and labour law in Europe and Japan (not researched). AI decision support touching HCP-facing content falls under promotional rules; the hypothesis assumes advise-only. Responsible-AI governance is thin in the bet.
Low exposure to competitor action, and it limits wasted spend on the other AI bets. Nothing a rival does changes its value.

Executing during a CEO transition, 4,500 role reductions and about JPY 359bn of restructuring expense over three years (128.1 + 70.8 + 160.0, council arithmetic) puts the morale risk the bet names on the bet itself. Owner conflict: CFO.

disagreements.text: Technology (support) versus Scientific (conditional): the platform can be built cheaply, but nobody can show that a data layer improves any decision outcome; ARCH's outcome is a preprint and Takeda's 30% claim is one interview. The councils disagree on whether low engineering risk is enough to proceed before IVB-001.

Capital (support) versus Commercial (conditional): capital sees a USD 200m low-risk enabler; commercial sees no revenue line and a data asset that cannot match a competitor's USD 1bn+ experimental data.

Takeda execution (support) versus Red team (oppose): the CEO's plasma heritage and the 270+ centre network make it Takeda's most executable bet, but the red team rejects the 'unique data' premise because plasma peers were never in the comparison set.
Capital (conditional on tranche) versus the strategy's own stage-gate table: the stage-gate file lists USD 435m of capital at risk, USD 5m more than the USD 430m bet size.

Technology and Takeda execution (support) versus Capital (oppose): capability is proven and in-house, but USD 500m for a 5-30% second-asset probability, paying off after the Entyvio window, is the weakest risk-adjusted use of scarce capital in the funded set.

Commercial and Capital (support) versus Red team (conditional): the spend is cheap against exposure, but the red team doubts contracting can retain revenue (Humira kept 97% volume and still lost 78.6% in three years). The councils agree to spend, and disagree on what the spend can achieve.

Scientific and Capital (support) versus Commercial and Red team (conditional): the clinical evidence is the best in the set, while the psoriasis market already contains an approved oral IL-23 with head-to-head claims.

Takeda execution (conditional, deal flow is a strength) versus Capital and Commercial (oppose): the engine is sized below one Innovent-type licence and pays off after the Entyvio window. The councils disagree on whether the proven BD capability should be pointed at early options or at mid-size Phase 2/3 licences.

Capital (conditional, small option) versus Commercial and Red team (oppose): cost is low but the differentiation claim is rejected because rivals hold the same or larger alliances. Technology flags that the prerequisite gates BET-01 and BET-09 are not wired into the roadmap before the Nabla window.
Capital and Execution (support) versus Commercial and Red team (conditional): near-free parity versus a permanent follower position in consortia that AbbVie and J&J lead.

Technology and Capital (support) versus Red team (conditional): the rent decision is technically and financially clean, but the red team argues the 'owned labs fail' evidence is weaker than the bet states.
Five councils endorse REJECT; the red team endorses zero spend but disputes the evidence, because Lilly's 2026 joint lab suggests it is re-investing in owned wet labs.

Technology and Execution (support) versus Commercial (conditional): the device capability exists, but moving patients to SC places them in the PBM channel where biosimilar templates apply, which works against BET-04.
Technology (support) versus Scientific, Capital and Execution (conditional): measurement is easy, but USD 100m is large for an experiment, and the pilot (2027 H2) follows an August 2026 approval.

Red team (support the DEFER) versus Commercial, Capital and Execution (oppose): all agree not to build now; three councils want the USD 80m removed from the envelope because DEFER bets elsewhere (BET-15) carry zero.

Capital (conditional) versus Red team (oppose): capital shows a USD 5bn purchase already breaches the 3.0x ceiling by arithmetic, so DEFER is really REJECT for now. The red team argues the opposite, that Takeda needs a funded bridge and waiting means losing assets to AbbVie and J&J.

Red team and Technology (support) versus Scientific, Commercial, Regulatory and Execution (conditional): everyone likes the discipline; four councils doubt the measurement can be independent when the CFO owns it and the savings target.

unreviewed.reason: BET-18 was proposed by the council's own decision memo (row 1 of the Director decision record) and added in strategy v2; no independent council review exists yet. Treat all seven council verdicts as pending; red-team scrutiny of the licensing channel is the first task of the next session.

items.text: ASM-024 (Entyvio erosion of 40-80% over three years) is bracketed by Eylea (-42% in one year) and Humira (-78.6% over three years). Both are different products with different channels. Neither is an intravenous infused biologic, so the bracket has no analogue for Entyvio's actual route of administration.

ASM-025 puts first meaningful US Entyvio biosimilar entry at 2031 (range 2030-2032). The range excludes entry in 2027-2029. Two biosimilar BLAs are under FDA review (one decision expected Q1 2027 per trade reporting), the reference product was first approved on 2014-05-20, and Takeda says biosimilars launching before the 2032 patent dates must address infringement and validity. Under the statutory 12-year reference-product exclusivity (a rule outside the registry, to be verified), the regulatory barrier would already have lapsed in May 2026, leaving patents as the only barrier. Playbook milestone RM-026 (2029 H2) would be late if entry were earlier.

The Entyvio exposure arithmetic applies ASM-024 to the global JPY 958.0bn. The US was JPY 351.8bn of JPY 541.7bn Entyvio sales in H1 FY2026 (about 65%, council arithmetic). First-entry erosion is a US event, so the three-year window is overstated on the global base, while ex-US erosion follows later and is absent from the table.

ASM-020, ASM-021, ASM-022 and ASM-028 (0.65, 0.15, 0.6, 0.1) are judgment, not data. Takeda's own R&D Day deck cites PTRS above 70% for the late-stage set, against ASM-022 at 0.6; neither is anchored. The capital ranking of bets uses these numbers, so the ranking is only as good as the judgment.

ASM-033 sets 3.0x adjusted net debt to EBITDA as the leverage ceiling for any USD 5bn+ purchase. It is not a Takeda policy. Council arithmetic: JPY 3,817.6bn plus JPY 750bn (USD 5bn at ASM-001) over JPY 1,457.2bn is 3.13x, and 3.41x if the JPY 403.5bn Amitiza provision is also debt-funded. The trigger is unmet by arithmetic before any asset is named.

ASM-034 is labelled a planning 'range' but holds one value, the JPY 403.5bn provision. At JPY 152 per USD it equals three times the USD 884.9m single damages (council arithmetic, consistent with, not confirmed by, Takeda's disclosure). The third-party-payor class, interest, fees and any appeal outcome are not in the number, so the provision is a base case, not a downside.

ASM-002 to ASM-004 are sums of bet-level sizings, not a top-down envelope. The 'constrained' case is set at 54% of balanced by convention. No Takeda technology or strategic-bet budget is public (IVB-014), so envelope totals could be off by a multiple.

ASM-106 sizes the option engine at USD 700m over 14 years, anchored on ADARx (USD 335m upfront) and Innovent (USD 1.2bn upfront including USD 100m equity). A single Innovent-type deal exceeds the whole engine. Either the engine excludes Takeda's real licence path or the anchor is mis-scaled.

ASM-031 (a 2% yield or cost improvement as the pilot pass mark, range 1-4%) has no economic anchor. Without cost per litre, the value of a 2% gain, and therefore whether USD 350m of follow-on is justified, cannot be computed.

ASM-101 sizes the data layer at USD 200m by reference to ARCH, built by fewer than ten staff plus contractors. ARCH's total cost is not disclosed, so the anchor supports an order of magnitude, not a number.

Six bets carry confidence 'evidence_backed' (BET-04, 05, 08, 09, 11, 16) while their load-bearing recommendation claims are PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED or NEEDS_MORE_RESEARCH (CLM-011054, 011065, 011066, 011072, 011073, 007053). The A10-bis scorecard already flagged seven recommendations labelled EVIDENCE_BACKED but registered PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED.

Most 'evidence' for the AI, data, plasma, orexin, registry and launch-pathway bets is the registry's own A11_strategy HYPOTHESIS or INTERPRETATION claims (CLM-011027 to CLM-011087), which carry NEEDS_MORE_RESEARCH or PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED status. Citing them as support is circular: they are hypotheses generated by the same strategy process.

The BET-04 premise that payer contracting can retain revenue assumes Entyvio sits in the contractable pharmacy channel. The registry has no claim on Entyvio's medical-benefit versus pharmacy-benefit mix. All three analogues (Humira, Stelara, Zepbound) are self-administered pharmacy-benefit products.

The exposure arithmetic shows 'if defence retains 10 points of erosion the value is about JPY 96bn a year'. No lever, evidence or analogue shows that any contracting posture retains 10 points. The figure illustrates scale and could be read as an expected benefit.

'Plasma is capacity-bound' rests on Lilly's tirzepatide shortage record. Takeda's own H1 FY2026 plasma revenue is -1.5% at constant rates, and no capacity-utilisation datum is public. The argument may be inverted: demand, pricing or collection rates may bind.

ASM-103 treats USD 500m of orexin spend as incremental to base R&D (ASM-035). The Shonan orexin discovery team already sits in base R&D of JPY 675.9bn, so the incremental share cannot be verified from public data.

The hypothesis that launch pathways govern oveporexton uptake is generalised from Spravato (site certification) and Carvykti (capacity). Narcolepsy type 1 is diagnosed and treated by sleep specialists, a population and referral pattern not examined in the registry.
ASM-117 assumes baselines can be set for AI use cases. J&J's published precedent (900 use cases reviewed, 10-15% drive about 80% of value) is a single CIO interview and carries no method.
How many AI and data products run in production at Takeda, with what users and what measured outcomes? Until IVB-001 is answered, BET-01 cannot be classified as a thin extension or a large build.
What is Entyvio's net price, persistence and benefit-channel split by payer segment, and what is the internal erosion curve? These decide whether the BET-04 lever exists (IVB-004).

What are Takeda's internal probabilities of success and launch forecasts for zasocitinib, oveporexton and rusfertide, and what was the FDA action date for zasocitinib under Priority Review (IVB-005)? The registry holds neither.
What are plasma yield per centre and cost per litre, and what is fractionation utilisation after the USD 230m expansion (IVB-006)?

What is the final Amitiza judgment, trebling, appeal path and cash timing, and was the JPY 403.5bn provision already counted in 'adjusted' net debt (IVB-012)? Leverage headroom for every large decision depends on it.
What is the scope, size and track record of Takeda Ventures and the Center for External Innovation (IVB-007)? The option engine assumes an organisation the registry cannot see.
What is Takeda's early-pipeline depth beyond the six late-stage programmes (IVB-008) and which competitors run orexin agonists in which phase? Neither is in the registry.
Which payments to Nabla and Iambic are committed upfront versus contingent, who owns the data fed to partner models, and what stop rules are in the contracts? The registry has only press terms.
What are Takeda's current internal cost per data point and turnaround for the assays it would rent (IVB-002)? The gate compares a CRO price against a baseline that is not known.
When did or will oveporexton become commercially available after the DEA scheduling decision, and what is the early prescription-to-first-dose time? The pilot date (2027 H2) depends on it.
What share of the JPY 200bn savings is attributed to technology versus headcount (IVB-003), and who certifies the attribution?
Does SC conversion retain net price and patients after biosimilar entry, or does it move patients into the pharmacy-benefit channel where PBM templates apply? No data exist (IVB-004).

Morphic deal value: USD 3.2bn (Reuters headline), USD 2.55bn (audited acquired IPR&D charge) and USD 3.35bn (cash paid per the 10-K) measure different things. A10 proposed keeping all three with a basis note; the registry has not yet recorded it as a conflict.

Lilly's robotic lab: BiopharmaTrend dates the Life Sciences Studio to 2017 (USD 90m); a Fierce snippet implies about 2020; the Strateos link and 2020 launch date are unsupported by any cited page; a Fierce snippet says Lilly sold 'a majority', not all. The reason for the sale is undisclosed. BET-09 and BET-10 lean on this evidence.
Takeda restructuring cost: about JPY 150bn (March 2026), JPY 170.0bn (original FY2026 forecast, May 2026) and JPY 160.0bn (revised, October 2026). CLM-005078 still mis-describes 170bn as trade press.
Cell-therapy impairment: JPY 58.0bn (October 2025 expectation) versus JPY 58.2bn (recognised in the FY2025 20-F). Not a contradiction, but several strategy files originally cited the earlier figure.

OTTAVA 'first commercial installation': the registry claim says completed on 2026-11-19, but J&J's release uses future tense. The De Novo grant date also differs by one day between claims (2026-07-21 FDA record versus 07-22). The strategy (BET-11 counter-example) uses it only as announced.

AI maturity: CLM-006054 and the master comparison say no company-level AI initiative shows a demonstrated outcome, while CLM-014073 (a former CEO's interview estimate of about 30% shorter narcolepsy development, no baseline or method) was first tagged DEMONSTRATED_OUTCOME. The A10-bis audit retagged it PILOT, so the registry now agrees. The strategy's statement that no competitor shows independent outcomes remains correct only in the narrower form A10 allows: the audit says CLM-006054's original wording is stronger than the sources support, so read it as 'none found in the sources opened'.

Zepbound exclusion: BET-04 and the LOE strategy cite 'about 11 months' with CLM-007011, but that claim records an 11% share-price fall on the announcement, not a duration. CVS restored Zepbound from 1 October 2026 (CLM-007013), about 15 months after the 1 July 2025 removal.

Medicare obesity-drug access: from 'as early as 1 April 2026' (Lilly release) versus 'by 1 July 2026' (10-K). Unresolved; no CMS primary document opened. It bears on SCN-3 timing assumptions about government pricing agreements.

NVIDIA CUDA developers: more than 11 million (company blog) versus over 7.5 million (10-K, different definition, ten months apart). The strategy's CUDA-flywheel analogy (BET-08, BET-14) depends on developer scale, and the audited figure is lower.

AbbVie ImmunoGen plus Cerevel: USD 18.5bn is consideration; USD 17.5bn is net of cash; ImmunoGen alone is USD 10.1bn announced, USD 9.8bn consideration and USD 9.2bn net. The bets use the net figures and the J&J USD 17.5bn is also net. Cross-company deal values remain invalid to add.

Debt basis: the statement text of CLM-003042 and the XBRL series CLM-000066 to CLM-000070 still reads non-current, but the registry correction field (A10) says the values include the current portion (AbbVie total USD 64,503m versus non-current USD 58,941m in CLM-000287). Anyone reading statement text without the correction field will misstate AbbVie or J&J leverage; leverage statements should name a basis.
AbbVie Ventures origin: 2009 versus about 2015. Unresolved; both rest on snippets. It bears on the BD-engine benchmark in BET-06 only weakly.

EXCLAIM-2: Takeda withdrew EXKIVITY in October 2023 after the trial missed its primary endpoint, yet the registry record shows primary completion on 2026-09-22. The registry date postdates the disclosure and must not be used to date the trial miss. Same pattern for abemaciclib CYCLONE 2.

Entyvio biosimilars: the registry holds the AVT16 FDA decision (Q1 2027) only as trade reporting, and the 2014 approval date only as an FDA review-document snippet. The 'exclusivity status unconfirmed' note means ASM-025 cannot be tested against a primary record such as the Purple Book.

J&J's 2.6x enrolment claim is one CIO sentence with 'up to' wording and no baseline; CLM-006022 course completions were retagged as a training metric. J&J AI claims are self-reported across the registry.

AISB performance: Apheris reports about 10 points better pose accuracy and 11 points better interface quality on 1,056 private held-out structures, organiser-run and not peer reviewed. The strategy cites it as part of an evidence_backed bet.
IVB-014: Takeda's approved multi-year technology and strategic-bet envelope is not public. Every dollar figure in the strategy is an ASSUMPTION and the envelope could differ by a multiple.
IVB-001: inventory of AI and data products in production versus pilot, users and outcomes.
IVB-002: lab automation and robotics footprint at Shonan, Boston and Vienna. The 'no evidence' finding is a public-evidence gap, not a finding of absence.
IVB-003: realised versus targeted savings and the technology share of the JPY 200bn programme.
IVB-004: Entyvio erosion scenarios, subcutaneous share and patent-litigation posture; rebate and contracting details are undisclosed per Takeda's 20-F.
IVB-005: internal probability of success and launch forecasts.
IVB-006: plasma yield per centre, cost per litre and fractionation automation. No plasma-peer benchmark is in the registry either.
IVB-007: scope of Takeda Ventures and the Center for External Innovation.
IVB-008: early-pipeline depth beyond six late-stage programmes. Takeda's pipeline page asset table (a PDF) and the Annual Integrated Report body were not opened.
IVB-010: use of AI models in target selection and clinical operations, and alliance results.
IVB-011: current FDA and EMA inspection status of Hikari and other sites, which bears on BET-02 automation validation and BET-05 launch timing.
IVB-012: Amitiza judgment timing, trebling, reserve adequacy and cash plan.
IVB-013: patient-assistance and market-access inventory; no company publishes adherence, persistence or time-to-therapy outcomes.

Not in the registry at all: plasma-industry peers (CSL Behring, Grifols, Octapharma and others), orexin-agonist competitors, Entyvio benefit-channel mix, EU and Japan policy beyond NHI, antitrust review of large transactions, and the Lilly-NVIDIA lab's operating status. Each limits a specific council verdict.

Lilly's Life Sciences Studio (an owned cloud robotic lab) was divested to the CRO Arctoris in 2024 and now operates as a service. No discovery outcome from it appears in any source opened. The reason for the sale is undisclosed, so it warns against owned automation but does not prove the model failed.

Zymergen paired automation and machine learning, sold to Ginkgo at about one-tenth of its IPO valuation after USD 1.2bn of cumulative net losses and a discontinued first product. It is an industrial-biotech company, so it warns about commercial risk of automated biofoundries, not about drug-discovery automation specifically.

Recursion ended four of its 11 programmes in May 2025 after a long-term extension did not sustain early signal; Exscientia (EXS-21546) and BenevolentAI programmes were discontinued; cited AI-origin Phase 2 success is about the same as conventional. These are the nearest AI-first company failures to the bet.

Insilico's rentosertib is the best AI-origin result in the registry (Phase IIa FVC signal, 71 patients, 12 weeks) and it carried seven liver-related discontinuations. A positive signal does not remove the standard safety risk.

AbbVie's emraclidine (Cerevel) missed both Phase 2 EMPOWER trials and cost a USD 4.5bn impairment, 24% of the USD 18.5bn paid for ImmunoGen and Cerevel. J&J's aticaprant Phase 3 stopped for insufficient efficacy. Neuroscience is the common failure site among AbbVie, J&J and Takeda.

Takeda's own orexin first attempt, TAK-994, was stopped for a liver-related signal in 2021, and soticlestat missed Phase 3 in 2024 (JPY 21.5bn impairment). The second asset is therefore not assured by the first approval.

Option and licence structures at Takeda have ended: Denali (April 2026), Neurocrine (March 2025), Maverick programmes (JPY 27.8bn impairment). Lilly discontinued DICE's lead asset the year after buying it, and AbbVie wrote Cerevel down 54%. No option from the window has produced an approved product.
Takeda's cell-therapy exit (JPY 58.2bn gamma-delta T-cell platform) shows that a new-modality bet can be written off after a decade. BET-06 asks for new-modality exposure again, through options.

J&J OTTAVA took a USD 0.9bn partial impairment in 2021 for development delays and only received De Novo authorisation in July 2026. Device robotics is a counter-example to the Intuitive pull-through analogy, although BET-11 is a drug-device bet.

Pear Therapeutics filed for Chapter 11 in April 2023 even though commentary says its clinical evidence was strong. AbbVie reversed its revised Allē loyalty programme within months and Botox Cosmetic then fell 11%.

Humira's contracting defence worked on volume (at least 97% to March 2024) and failed on revenue (U.S. Humira -35% in 2023, -41% in 2024, -57% in 2025). A co-branded private-label route delayed, not prevented, the loss.

Google dissolved its unified Google Health division in about three years (snippet-level source). It is a weak analogue, but it shows that a large data and AI platform in healthcare does not guarantee product-market fit.

Lilly's TuneLab has distribution to 1,300+ Benchling customers but no disclosed uptake or retraining counts; the only usage figure is a single vendor blog. A productised model platform has no demonstrated customer demand to copy.

Inspection-driven launch delays at Lilly (lebrikizumab CRL) and AbbVie (ABBV-951 second CRL) warn against plans that assume approval dates follow clinical data. Takeda's own warning letter history is documented.

Lilly's 2024 sale of the Studio and its 2026 joint lab with NVIDIA (up to USD 1bn) can be read as re-platforming at larger scale, which reverses the lesson the strategy draws ('owned labs fail'). Under that reading renting is a way to be a follower.

Entyvio's FY2025 growth (+4.8%) and H1 FY2026 growth (+2.7% CER) can be read as proof the franchise is resilient before entry, in which case early spend is premature. The dated exposure argues the reverse. The registry cannot settle which reading holds.

The Humira lesson can be read two ways: contracting retained volume (97% for 14 months), or contracting failed because net price collapsed anyway. The strategy uses it as a model for defence; a contrary reading treats it as a warning that volume defence is not revenue defence.

Plasma-derived revenue -1.5% at constant rates in H1 FY2026 can mean a mature, demand-bound category (automation saves cost only) rather than a capacity-bound one (automation unlocks revenue). The strategy's 'capacity' reading is favourable to the bet.

The strategy treats zasocitinib as replacement revenue. It can equally be read as a second concentration risk: a single oral TYK2 product with a USD 4bn price carries two USD 1bn milestones and enters a class where J&J has an approved oral comparator.

The rationale 'options are safer than purchases' can be reversed: AbbVie's option stream and Lilly's expensed IPR&D produced no approvals by the cutoff, while Takeda's approved late-stage assets came from licensed Phase 2/3 programmes (Protagonist, Nimbus). Phase 2/3 licensing, not options, is the evidenced path.

Takeda's AI partnerships may be better read as data bets than as AI bets: the scarce input is proprietary assay and clinical data, and the partner model is replaceable. That makes BET-07 part of BET-01 and BET-09.
AISB membership can be read as a sign that Takeda has data worth contributing (five pharmas, 20,000 structures) or as a sign it is a junior member (absent from the Bind founding list).

Takeda's FY2025 R&D fell to JPY 675.9bn from JPY 730.2bn because programmes ended and mezagitamab co-funding began. That can be read as discipline or as retrenchment ahead of the pipeline refill gap. The same reading applies to the 160bn restructuring programme.
'DEFER' can be read as prudence (leverage 2.6x, Amitiza) or as inaction while AbbVie and J&J buy bridges. The council arithmetic shows the trigger is already unmet, so DEFER may be a polite REJECT.

The strategy treats Entyvio as the single exposure to defend (21% of revenue). Vyvanse removed about JPY 220bn of annual revenue in two years, Trintellix faces generics after December 2026 and Takhzyro's patent runs to January 2036. Together the 2026-2030 erosion may exceed Entyvio's, and the bets address only one.
Registry-based evidence for rare-disease or plasma products may come more cheaply from patient-organisation partnerships and existing hub data (BET-12) than from a neutral registry vehicle.

Efficacy statements for Takeda's 2026 approvals and zasocitinib are company-reported. Source tiers: 71 of 83 A5 Takeda claims were flagged single_interested_source, and independent_corroboration is populated on only two of 1,401 registry claims (CLM-000280, CLM-000283).

Cross-company comparisons used by the bets are bounded by the audit: shares of revenue from post-2021 molecules, deal-value sums and capex comparisons are invalid. A reader should not rank Takeda against Lilly, J&J or AbbVie from the strategy files.

Mechanism analogies (NVIDIA, SpaceX, Regeneron, TSMC, AWS, Intuitive, Flatiron) generate hypotheses and several are snippet-level. SpaceX's NASA source states the cause of the cost gap is not isolated; CUDA's cost claim is one interested speaker; Roche's realised value from Flatiron is not in the registry.
BET-04 is the only bet with fixed external dates (January 2028, biosimilar reviews, 2032 patents). Its evidence is the strongest in the set but its mechanism is the least tested at Takeda.

The REJECT recommendations (BET-10, BET-14, BET-16) are the best-evidenced decisions because they rest on absence of demonstrated benefit and on structural mismatch. Absence of evidence is not evidence of failure; the sample is small and the search was limited.
Patient-support programme evidence at every company is enrolment or access counts. Any design for BET-12 starts without a published benchmark.

Stage-gate capital at risk is a convention (ASM-037) and sums to USD 5m more than the bet size for BET-02, BET-07, BET-09 and BET-11 (USD 20m in total). BET-15's USD 5,000m gate exposure sits outside every portfolio.

Competitor claims about AI metrics (J&J 2.6x, 10-15% of use cases, 47,000 course completions; Takeda 63.4% usage; Nabla three to four weeks) are self-reported or interview-sourced. None is independent.

Takeda's FY runs April-March; the strategy cutoff is 2026-11-21 and roughly half of FY2026 is a forecast. JPY-to-USD conversions use 150 (ASM-001) for sizing only; the Amitiza arithmetic implies about JPY 152. Exchange-rate movement changes every USD-denominated envelope against JPY figures.

lessons.area: Manufacturing capacity as the binding constraint on a blockbuster
lessons.what_they_did: Lilly raised capex from USD 1.3bn (FY2021) to USD 7.8bn (FY2025) and announced more than USD 50bn of U.S. commitments after tirzepatide supply fell short; the FDA removed tirzepatide from the shortage list on 2024-10-02. Most announced sites are still pre-operating, with operating evidence only for Concord, Kinsale and the Lebanon genetic-medicine plant.
lessons.why: Takeda's plasma-derived therapies are capacity-bound (collection centres and fractionation) and it has a USD 230m Los Angeles expansion, so the capacity logic transfers. The lesson to copy is to track operating capacity, not announced capacity. Takeda's FY2025 capex of JPY 426.9bn includes intangible assets and is not comparable with Lilly's property, plant and equipment capex.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_STRENGTH (class 2: plasma network and PDT manufacturing)

lessons.area: Cash-pay direct-to-patient channel
lessons.what_they_did: Lilly launched LillyDirect on 2024-01-04, sold Zepbound self-pay vials from August 2024 and cut prices on 2025-12-01 to USD 299 / 399 / 449. The company says over 1 million patients accessed treatments through it in 2025; the 10-K gives no dollar share, and copay-accumulator and anti-kickback limits restrict combining discounts with insurance.
lessons.why: Cash-pay scaled in an uninsured-gap category (obesity). Takeda's main products are infused or specialty-distributed biologics and plasma therapies sold through payer coverage and hubs, so a cash channel fits poorly. Home and subcutaneous conversion (LES-21) is the better-evidenced mechanism.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EVIDENCE_GAP (class 14: patient services and market access)

lessons.area: Data-for-access platform (federated learning)
lessons.what_they_did: Lilly launched TuneLab on 2025-09-09, giving selected biotechs access to Lilly-trained ADMET and safety models in exchange for federated data contributions, with Benchling distribution to more than 1,300 customers opt-in later in 2026. No uptake, retraining count or scientific outcome is disclosed.
lessons.why: Takeda is already in a multi-pharma federated consortium (AISB) and could be a data-for-models participant, which is a cheaper position than building a rival platform. The platform's value is unproven, so participation should wait for independent results.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED (class 9: enterprise data and AI platform, outcomes unproven)

lessons.area: Owned robotic lab versus rented automation
lessons.what_they_did: Lilly built a remote robotic laboratory (Life Sciences Studio) and divested it to the CRO Arctoris in 2024; the reason is undisclosed. Zymergen, an owned biofoundry, was sold at about one-tenth of its IPO-era valuation. The NVIDIA-Lilly co-innovation lab announced in January 2026 is at concept stage.
lessons.why: The evidence favours buying automation as a service and gating AI-biotech deals on first-in-human data rather than owning a robotic lab. Takeda has no public lab-automation evidence, so there is nothing to retreat from.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EVIDENCE_GAP (class 11: lab automation and robotics)

lessons.area: Growth concentration, price erosion and payer leverage
lessons.what_they_did: Tirzepatide reached 56.0% of Lilly's FY2025 revenue (15.6% in FY2023). Realised prices fell 5% in Q4 2025 and 15% in Q3 2026 while volume rose 46% and 53%; CVS Caremark removed Zepbound for about 11 months; Trulicity and Verzenio face Medicare-set prices from 2028.
lessons.why: Entyvio is 21% of Takeda's revenue, faces Medicare negotiation from 2028 and a coming biosimilar event. Lilly's record shows that volume growth in a dominant franchise comes with net-price pressure and PBM leverage, so Takeda should plan for price erosion in its core franchise, not only for volume loss.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_STRENGTH (class 1: GI and immunology franchise)

lessons.area: Steady cadence of early-asset purchases versus a concentrated bet
lessons.what_they_did: Lilly expensed USD 3.8bn, 3.3bn and 2.9bn of acquired IPR&D in 2023-2025 (Morphic USD 2,548.5m, DICE USD 1,915.5m); none of those assets had been approved in the sources reviewed, and DICE's lead asset was discontinued in 2024.
lessons.why: A cadence of purchases keeps options open but had produced no approval by cutoff. Takeda's one large asset purchase (Nimbus, February 2023) reached an accepted NDA in September 2026, so the two models have different risk profiles; Takeda's organisation for external innovation is not documented publicly.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_STRENGTH (class 5: external innovation and BD, deal flow); organisation EVIDENCE_GAP

lessons.area: Successor sequencing before the cliff
lessons.what_they_did: J&J had TREMFYA (IL-23) on the market with Crohn's and UC labels and approved the oral IL-23 peptide ICOTYDE on about 2026-03-17. In FY2025 Tremfya grew USD 1,485m, offsetting about 35% of Stelara's USD 4,283m loss, yet Immunology still fell 11.8%.
lessons.why: The mechanism requires a successor in the same prescriber base launched years before the loss. Takeda's zasocitinib is an oral TYK2 inhibitor in psoriasis, not a successor to Entyvio in gastroenterology, so it replaces revenue but not the franchise. J&J's record also shows that even a pre-launched successor offsets only part of the loss in the first year.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED (class 7: LOE replacement)

lessons.area: Debt-funded acquisition bridge
lessons.what_they_did: J&J acquired businesses for USD 15.1bn (FY2024) and USD 17.5bn (FY2025) net of cash; net debt rose from USD 2.1bn (FY2021) to USD 27.8bn (FY2025) while it paid about USD 12.4bn of dividends and USD 6.0bn of buybacks in FY2025.
lessons.why: J&J's bridge rests on USD 24.5bn of operating cash flow and a large MedTech and pharma base. Takeda stated no significant acquisitions in three years, carries a company-defined adjusted leverage ratio (2.6x, not verified by the audit) and has a JPY 403.5bn Amitiza provision, so its bridge capacity depends on legal cash timing that is not public.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED (class 16: cost transformation) with class 5 deal flow

lessons.area: Claimed pharma and MedTech synergy
lessons.what_they_did: J&J asserts that pairing Abiomed, Biosense Webster and Shockwave creates cardiovascular leadership, but no cross-segment revenue synergy is disclosed. MedTech earns a 12.2% segment margin against 36.9% for Innovative Medicine, and J&J announced the Orthopaedics separation on 2025-10-14.
lessons.why: Takeda has no MedTech segment, so the structure does not apply. The transferable point is to test a claimed combination synergy against segment margins and disclosed revenue links before building strategy on it.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: NOT_APPLICABLE (Takeda has no MedTech segment; six key business areas)

lessons.area: Inspection findings, not clinical data, behind approval delays
lessons.what_they_did: Lilly's lebrikizumab CRL (October 2023) came from third-party manufacturer inspection findings, with no concern on clinical data, safety or label; lebrikizumab was approved as Ebglyss on 2024-09-13. AbbVie's second ABBV-951 CRL (June 2024) also cited third-party manufacturer observations.
lessons.why: Takeda's baseline already records a 2020 FDA warning letter at Hikari with a Leuprorelin supply shortage. Launch timing for its 2026 approvals and the zasocitinib NDA depends on site inspection status, including third-party sites.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED (class 12: manufacturing quality, one documented failure)

lessons.area: Litigation overhang and reserve volatility
lessons.what_they_did: J&J's talc subsidiaries filed three Chapter 11 petitions (two dismissed, Red River not confirmed on 2025-03-31); J&J reversed about USD 7bn of reserve, held about USD 3.4bn at FY2025 end, then proposed a USD 5.5bn ovarian resolution on 2026-07-27 that needs 95% participation. Plaintiff counsel says the cost could reach USD 7bn or more.
lessons.why: Talc is product liability and Takeda's AMITIZA case is pay-for-delay antitrust, so legal mechanics differ. The transferable point is that reserve and settlement estimates moved by billions within a year at J&J; Takeda's JPY 403.5bn provision follows a jury verdict it intends to appeal, and the final judgement and cash timing are not public.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: NOT_APPLICABLE (legal exposure is not a baseline capability class)

lessons.area: Self-reported AI metrics without baselines
lessons.what_they_did: J&J's CIO reported nearly 900 gen-AI use cases reviewed, trial-site recommendations with 'up to 2.6x' enrolment, and 47,000 employees completing a gen-AI course. The enrolment figure has no baseline or method, and course completions are a training metric. The audit retagged both.
lessons.why: Takeda's own reported measures (63.4% of the workforce actively using gen-AI tools; a vendor-hosted agent platform) are also usage or self-report measures. Takeda should define outcome baselines (time saved, cycle time, cost) before treating usage as value.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED (class 9: enterprise data and AI platform, outcomes unproven)

lessons.area: Extend the successor across the incumbent's indications before the cliff
lessons.what_they_did: Skyrizi and Rinvoq gained psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's, ulcerative colitis and atopic dermatitis labels between 2022 and 2025 and, with head-to-head data, covered Humira's major indications. Together they rose from USD 7,687m (2022) to USD 25,866m (2025) against a Humira loss of USD 16,697m.
lessons.why: Takeda has psoriatic arthritis Phase 3 studies for zasocitinib running to May 2027 and a head-to-head Phase 3 win over deucravacitinib, which is the same pattern of indication breadth and comparative data. The AbbVie successors were already marketed before the cliff; Takeda's are not yet.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED (class 7: LOE replacement)

lessons.area: Contracting defence against PBM-driven biosimilar substitution
lessons.what_they_did: AbbVie kept at least 97% of adalimumab volume through March 2024 with rebate-for-access contracts, then supplied a co-branded Humira to CVS's Cordavis when Caremark removed Humira from template formularies on 2024-04-01; U.S. Humira revenue still fell 41% in 2024 and 57% in 2025.
lessons.why: PBM private labels now handle large biosimilar events (nine Stelara biosimilars by July 2025, four from PBM-affiliated labels), so payer contracting depth matters as much as patents. Takeda has no public evidence on rebate or contracting structure, and two Entyvio biosimilar BLAs are under FDA review.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EVIDENCE_GAP (class 14: patient services and market access) with class 1 GI franchise

lessons.area: Size acquisitions to survive a write-down
lessons.what_they_did: AbbVie recorded a USD 4.5bn impairment in Q4 2024 after emraclidine failed, 54% of the USD 8.3bn Cerevel net price. The same year's ImmunoGen purchase supplied a growing product (Elahere) and Cerevel's tavapadon was approved as Juvmo in September 2026.
lessons.why: Takeda's largest purchase (Nimbus, USD 4.0bn upfront) has the same single-asset risk profile and has so far delivered. Takeda's baseline already shows that stop decisions and write-downs (cell therapy, soticlestat) are absorbed; the lesson is to size any next large purchase so one failure does not breach leverage or dividend policy.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_STRENGTH (class 6: portfolio discipline, with write-down cost)

lessons.area: Settlement-based IP to convert patent dates into entry dates
lessons.what_they_did: AbbVie's September 2025 settlements with all Rinvoq generic filers mean no generic tablet entry is expected before April 2037, four years after the 2033 composition patent; Humira biosimilar entry was negotiated to 2023.
lessons.why: Entyvio patents expire in some cases in 2032 and third parties filed UK and Netherlands revocation actions in early 2026, so Takeda faces litigation rather than settled entry dates. What is transferable is the posture; the outcome depends on Takeda's litigation position, which is not public.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_BUT_UNDERDEVELOPED (class 7: LOE replacement)

lessons.area: Option and early-stage licence volume
lessons.what_they_did: AbbVie runs a yearly stream of USD 0.6bn to 1.0bn of early-stage upfronts and option deals (ADARx USD 335m upfront with up to USD 7.5bn of milestones; Gubra USD 350m; Ichnos USD 700m). None had produced an approved product by cutoff.
lessons.why: Takeda's Innovent arrangement (USD 1.2bn upfront including USD 100m equity, with an option) is the same shape on a smaller number of deals. The evidence does not show that volume produces approvals, and Takeda's external-innovation organisation is not documented in primary sources.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_STRENGTH (class 5: external innovation and BD, deal flow); organisation EVIDENCE_GAP

lessons.area: High variance of first-in-class psychiatry and neuroscience assets
lessons.what_they_did: AbbVie's emraclidine Phase 2 missed its primary endpoint in November 2024; J&J stopped aticaprant on insufficient efficacy in March 2025; Takeda's soticlestat Phase 3 missed in June 2024. Neuroscience and psychiatry is the common failure site across three companies in the window.
lessons.why: Takeda's oveporexton succeeded in a different neuroscience area (orexin, with discovery in Shonan) after TAK-994 was stopped in 2022 for liver safety. The lesson is to gate psychiatry and CNS assets on Phase 2 quality and placebo response, and not to infer that orexin success transfers to other CNS bets.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_STRENGTH (class 3: rare disease and orexin science)

lessons.area: Redesigning a patient or provider programme without a pilot
lessons.what_they_did: AbbVie launched a revised Alle loyalty programme in October 2024 and reinstated the original in early 2025 after providers found the new one too complex; U.S. Botox Cosmetic revenue fell 11% in 2025 on pricing from programme changes, lower share and lower demand.
lessons.why: Takeda has no aesthetics business, and Alle is a consumer loyalty scheme. The narrower point, that a support-programme redesign can cost share within months and should be piloted, applies to Takeda's Help at Hand and EntyvioConnect programmes, which have no public outcome data.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EVIDENCE_GAP (class 14: patient services and market access)

lessons.area: Packaging price concessions with tariff relief and investment pledges
lessons.what_they_did: Lilly (2025-11-06), J&J (2026-01-08) and AbbVie (2026-01-12) each announced a voluntary agreement pairing price or access concessions with tariff relief and a U.S. investment pledge (Lilly more than USD 50bn since 2020, J&J more than USD 55bn over four years, AbbVie USD 100bn over a decade).
lessons.why: Takeda's 20-F records MFN pricing and Japan's annual price revisions as risks and the registry holds no Takeda pledge or agreement. Whether such a package is available or advisable for Takeda cannot be judged from public evidence; the competitor agreements are company announcements, and their terms and realised value are not independently verified.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: NOT_APPLICABLE (policy engagement is not a baseline capability class)

lessons.area: Home and subcutaneous administration as a growth and defence mechanism
lessons.what_they_did: TREMFYA subcutaneous share gains accompanied USD 5,155m of FY2025 sales (+40.5%); Zepbound moved to vials and a KwikPen with self-pay pricing from USD 299.
lessons.why: This is the best-evidenced transferable mechanism for Takeda: the ENTYVIO subcutaneous pen is approved for UC (September 2023) and Crohn's disease (April 2024), the 20-F says it continues to drive uptake, and HYHUB needle-free Hyqvia transfer received FDA 510(k) clearance in July 2025. Effect on net price and erosion after biosimilar entry is not established.
lessons.takeda_baseline_class: EXISTING_STRENGTH (class 1: GI and immunology franchise)
